extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology (e.g., readers of Locke)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for judging when ideas (simple, complex, modes, substances) are true, false, right, or wrong; plus principles about how ideas become associated and how that produces (un)reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and Falsehood belong to Propositions, not to Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Though truth and falsehood properly belong only to PROPOSITIONS: yet IDEAS are oftentimes termed true or false (as words are used with latitude).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideas themselves, being bare appearances or perceptions in the mind, cannot simply be said to be true or false; when ideas are so called there is a tacit proposition (an affirmation or negation) that grounds that denomination. Evaluate alleged 'true' or 'false' ideas by the propositions/judgments that refer to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas and words may be 'true' in a metaphysical sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Both ideas and words may be said to be true, in a metaphysical sense of the word truth; as all other things that any way exist are said to be true, i.e. really to be such as they exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a different, broader sense of 'true' (existing/really being such) and is not the ordinary epistemic sense used when judging correctness of ideas in discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas as appearances in the mind are neither true nor false
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas being nothing but bare APPEARANCES, or perceptions in our minds, cannot properly and simply in themselves be said to be true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the idea of a centaur has no more falsehood in it when it appears in our minds than the name 'centaur' has falsehood when written or spoken. Do not call raw mental images 'true' or 'false' absent a judgment that connects them to something external.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas referred to anything extraneous may be called true or false
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the mind refers any of its ideas to anything extraneous to them, they are then capable to be called true or false, because the mind tacitly supposes their conformity to that thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common cases: (1) reference to other men's ideas (shared meanings); (2) reference to real existence (does the idea represent something real?); (3) reference to the real constitution/essence of a thing. When analysing truth-claims, make explicit which reference or standard is being used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three sorts of abstract ideas / nominal essences
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind has three sorts of abstract ideas or nominal essences: First, SIMPLE ideas (copies, yet adequate). Secondly, COMPLEX ideas of SUBSTANCES (ectypes/copies but not adequate). Thirdly, COMPLEX ideas of MODES AND RELATIONS (archetypes, originals, and adequate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to judge claims about adequacy/identity: simple ideas reliably represent the powers producing sensations; complex substance-ideas are typically incomplete; ideas of modes/relations are produced by the mind and so can be fully adequate to what the mind intends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas are (in ordinary sense) adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: SIMPLE ideas, which are copies, are certainly adequate because they are intended to express nothing but the power in things to produce in the mind such a sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the sensation of white produced by paper is perfectly adequate to that power. When evaluating notions grounded in simple sensory impressions, treat them as directly corresponding to the producing power and minimally susceptible to falsity relative to that producing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas of substances are inadequate/deficient
rubrics_metrics.description: COMPLEX ideas of SUBSTANCES are ectypes, copies too, but not perfect ones, not adequate: we cannot be sure that a collection of simple ideas we make of any substance exactly answers all that are in that substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the common complex idea of 'gold' (colour, weight, fusibility, ductility) omits innumerable other powers; thus claims that a complex idea fully captures an object's essence should be treated skeptically. Beware assuming that observed properties exhaust an object's essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas of modes and relations are archetypes and adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: COMPLEX ideas of MODES AND RELATIONS are originals and archetypes; being collections the mind itself puts together, each contains precisely all that the mind intends it should, and so cannot but be adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modes and relations are mental constructs: when evaluating conceptual definitions or putative essences of modes, check whether the mind's construction contains exactly the intended parts — if so, it is adequate by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names are often wrongly supposed to carry knowledge of essences
rubrics_metrics.description: Men commonly suppose that the name carried with it the knowledge of the species, or the essence of it; as if the name were the mark of the essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about meaning or essence, do not conflate having a name with having knowledge of the real essence. Probe for whether the 'abstract idea' attached to a name truly tracks the thing's constitution or is merely a convenient label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas are least liable to be false in reference to others' ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: SIMPLE IDEAS are least of all liable to be mistaken when judged by conformity to the ideas which other men have, because they are few and can be rectified by checking their objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In communicative contexts, give priority to grounding claims in simple ideas (sensory marks) when seeking intersubjective agreement; they are more robust to misapplication of names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas (esp. mixed modes) are most liable to be false in reference to others' ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: COMPLEX ideas are much more liable to be false in this respect; and the complex ideas of MIXED MODES, much more than those of substances, because definitions and collections are human-made and lack a sensible standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating disputes about justice, gratitude, virtue, etc., recognize that disagreement often stems from different abstract constructions (mixed modes). Clarify definitions rather than assume shared content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of substances false when they join simples not united in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of substances are false when they put together simple ideas which in the real existence of things have no union; e.g., joining a horse's shape with a dog's barking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag conceptual combinations that attribute jointly what never co-occurs in reality as false representations of substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of substances false when they separate inseparable simples (direct negation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas are false when, from any collection of simple ideas that do always exist together, there is separated, by a direct negation, any other simple idea which is constantly joined with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: treating gold's essential properties but explicitly denying a degree of fixedness that in reality accompanies them — this is a false complex idea. Evaluate definitions for illicit negations of inseparable properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of substances false when judged adequate though incomplete (omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas are false (or rather inadequate) when one judges a complex idea to be a perfect complete idea of a sort though it omits properties that are inseparable in reality (e.g., omitting fixedness or solubility in aqua regia from 'gold').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between falsehood (contradictory/illusory unions) and inadequacy by omission; challenge claims that a conceptual list is exhaustive when it plausibly omits inseparable features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth/Falsehood presuppose Affirmation or Negation (judgment required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth or Falsehood always supposes some JUDGMENT that the mind makes, or is supposed to make; for truth or falsehood being never without some affirmation or negation, it is not to be found but where signs are joined or separated according to the agreement of the things they stand for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing truth claims, look for the underlying propositions (explicit or tacit) that perform the affirming/denying; error often lies in an unwarranted tacit judgment rather than in raw ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas in themselves are better called Right or Wrong when referred
rubrics_metrics.description: Our ideas, considered as in the mind, may very fitly be called RIGHT or WRONG ideas, according as they agree or disagree to the patterns to which they are referred; but strictly TRUTH or FALSEHOOD belongs to propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'right/wrong' to discuss conformity of an idea to a referent or standard; reserve 'true/false' for propositional judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong connexion (association) of ideas causes unreasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is scarce any one that does not observe something extravagant in the opinions, reasonings, and actions of other men; this often springs from a wrong connexion of ideas — ideas that in themselves are not allied come to be so united by chance or custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing irrationality in arguments or behaviour, consider whether associations of ideas (habitual or accidental) rather than logical relations underlie the judgement. Tracing associative links can reveal root causes of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom and habit settle associative connections of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: This strong combination of ideas, not allied by nature, the mind makes in itself either voluntarily or by chance; CUSTOM settles habits of thinking in the understanding, as well as in the will and body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cognitive errors or entrenched beliefs by examining learned associative habits; interventions aimed at changing custom/habit (training, education) can reshape these connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some sympathies/antipathies are effects of associative pairing
rubrics_metrics.description: A great part of the sympathies and antipathies observable in men are attributable to accidental connexion of two ideas (e.g., surfeiting on honey causing nausea associated with the idea of honey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing affective responses or apparently irrational dislikes/likings, probe for historical associative origins rather than assuming natural or logical bases.
